Adhesion to and invasion of terminal ileum mucosa via M-cells of Peyer’s patches

qs.q: A histological slide of the small intestine shows prominent mucosal folds with numerous villi and crypts. Which feature distinguishes the ileum from the duodenum?
qs.e: Aggregated lymphoid follicles, known as Peyer's patches, are characteristic of the distal ileum.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with an ileal resection develops severe vitamin B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption. Which specific transporter mechanism in the terminal ileum is disrupted by this surgical intervention?
qs.e: Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via a specialized apical sodium-dependent bile acid co-transporter.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 29-year-old woman with Crohn's disease presents with an internal fistula communicating between the ileum and colon, accompanied by a localized intra-abdominal abscess. What is the characteristic pathological origin of most internal fistulas?
qs.e: Internal fistulas typically arise from local perforation of diseased bowel with an associated abscess rather than external surgical trauma. Iatrogenic causes predominantly result in external enterocutaneous fistulas.
qs.s: Intestinal and Enterocutaneous Fistulas: Classification and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 32-year-old man develops a lateral fistula from the side of the ileum following a penetrating abdominal injury, leaving partial bowel wall continuity intact. How is this distinct from an end fistula?
qs.e: An end fistula arises from complete discontinuity of the entire bowel diameter, whereas a lateral fistula arises from one side, leaving partial continuity. Both types can have varying outputs depending on their anatomical location.
qs.s: Intestinal and Enterocutaneous Fistulas: Classification and Management: MCQs

qs.q: During an exploratory laparotomy for suspected adhesive small bowel obstruction, a surgeon identifies a tight fibrous band constricting a segment of the ileum. After dividing the band, the surgeon must assess bowel viability before deciding whether to perform a resection. Which observation confirms that the affected bowel segment is non-viable?
o: Sluggish pink color return after warm saline application
Absent peristalsis, lack of arterial bleeding, and dark black wall
Presence of normal subserosal blood vessels with mild pallor
Active bleeding from the mesenteric border when gently scored
qs.e: Non-viable bowel is identified by a dark or black wall, absent peristalsis, loss of arterial bleeding from cut edges, and lack of Doppler signals. Sluggish but present color recovery and active bleeding indicate viable tissue that can be preserved.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: An infant with total colonic aganglionosis undergoes a specialized surgical correction where the ileum is anastomosed directly to the anus, accompanied by a side-to-side ileocolic anastomosis. What is the name of this procedure?
qs.e: Martin's procedure is specifically designed for total colonic aganglionosis by anastomosing the ileum to the anus with a side-to-side ileocolic anastomosis. The other procedures are standard or modified pull-throughs for shorter aganglionic segments.

qs.q: A 32-week preterm infant with unstable hemodynamics undergoes laparotomy for stage III necrotising enterocolitis. After resection of frankly necrotic ileum, the surgeon must decide how to manage the bowel ends. What is the most appropriate surgical strategy?
o: Construct a diverting enterostomy with a proximal mucous fistula
Perform a primary end‑to‑end anastomosis to re‑establish continuity
Use the clip‑and‑drop method to close abdomen without a stoma
Place a temporary intraluminal feeding tube across the resection
qs.e: In unstable infants, bringing out stomas avoids the high risk of anastomotic leak associated with primary repair. The clip-and-drop technique is reserved for cases of total bowel necrosis where no viable bowel remains to stoma.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

qs.q: A premature neonate undergoes extensive surgical resection for severe necrotising enterocolitis involving the terminal ileum. Which specific nutritional deficiency is most directly anticipated as a long-term consequence of this specific loss?
qs.e: Loss of the terminal ileum directly leads to vitamin B12 and bile salt deficiency. While fat-soluble vitamins can be poorly absorbed, bile salt and B12 malabsorption are tied specifically to the terminal ileum.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The ileum is the distal part of the small intestine, crucial for bile acid reabsorption and immune surveillance. Clinicians must recognize its role in malabsorption, Crohn’s disease, and surgical resections. Understanding its relations helps avoid iatrogenic injury.

sections.p: The ileum is the final segment of the small intestine, extending from the jejunoileal junction to the ileocecal valve. It is a key site for nutrient absorption and immune function.
It begins at the jejunoileal junction and ends at the ileocecal valve. The mucosa has villi and microvilli, and the submucosa contains lymphoid aggregates.
Adjacent structures include the cecum, appendix, and mesenteric vessels. The ileocecal valve separates it from the colon.
Supplied by the ileocolic artery (branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and drained by the ileocolic vein.

t.b: Assesses blood flow; low flow suggests ischemia

sections.p: Parasympathetic via vagus and pelvic splanchnic nerves; sympathetic via mesenteric plexus.
Absorbs bile acids, vitamin B12, and remaining nutrients. It also hosts immune cells that sample luminal antigens.
Common issues include Crohn’s disease, ischemia, and surgical resections. Complications can lead to malabsorption and strictures.
Remember the ileal brake: fat stimulates PYY release, slowing gastric emptying. In surgery, avoid damaging the ileocecal valve.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, signs of obstruction, or bloody diarrhea
Rapid weight loss with malabsorption symptoms

faq.a: Loss or dysfunction of ileal transporters, often due to Crohn’s disease or resection.

faq.q: How is Crohn’s disease diagnosed in the ileum?
faq.a: Endoscopy with biopsy showing transmural inflammation and granulomas; imaging shows strictures.

faq.q: Why is the ileum important for vitamin B12 absorption?
faq.a: Intrinsic factor–B12 complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors.
